results.note: All counts, RRs, z and p match Results ¶1. Editors' check, 95% CIs implied by RR and z: insomnia 1.45-1.78, initial 2.05-3.77, combined 2.13-4.15, sleep disorder 1.44-2.74; z = 183 would imply 2.94-3.00, so a misprint: do not derive.
Matches the subsection's 1st paragraph and the Figure 2 note; 'Egger's' comes from Methods › Statistical Analyses. Dots are observations: some trials contribute more than one.

results.corrected_extracted: Drug and placebo adverse-event rates were highly correlated (r = 0.89, p < 0.0001) and observed relative risks were close to those predicted from the placebo rate alone; citing Wernicke et al., the authors note that eliciting adverse events gives higher absolute rates in both groups, while spontaneous reporting more often gives larger relative risks; so relative risks should be read with absolute risks, which the review does not report in its text.
results.note: The eliciting statement is Wernicke et al.'s finding, cited in Discussion ¶9; it says 'more often' and names no questionnaires. Here, elicited vs spontaneous reporting did not predict the RR (Assessment of Potentially Confounding Variables ¶1).

results.corrected_extracted: Manuscript development funded by Ironshore Pharmaceuticals & Development, a subsidiary of Highland Therapeutics; two PharmDs from Ironshore assisted with data extraction and two authors are employees of Highland Therapeutics; the first author reported income or support from 13 companies, including Ironshore.
results.note: The paper never says a compared product is Ironshore's (HLD200 appears only in figure notes): drop or source it outside the anchor. Acknowledgements say the extractors were 'from' Ironshore. Added the first author's printed disclosure.

results.corrected_extracted: MDMA against placebo (2-factor analysis over treatment and recovery nights, df 1 and 6), treatment-night values: total sleep 310.6 (SEM 45.3) against 437.1 (8.1) minutes, F = 8.6, P = 0.026; latency to persistent sleep 112.3 (46.1) against 14.9 (5.0) minutes, F = 7.0, P = 0.038; stage 1 8.4 against 6.6%, F = 9.49, P = 0.022; REM 3.5 (2.1) against 19.2 (2.0)%, F = 14.28, P = 0.009, reduced on the treatment night only (interaction F = 23.70, P = 0.003); no effect on wake after persistent sleep, stage 2 (P = 0.267), stage 3/4 (P = 0.119) or REM latency (P = 0.589).
results.note: All numbers match Results ¶1 and Table 3. The measure is 'wake after persistent sleep', not wake after sleep onset; the F tests are the drug effect across treatment and recovery nights (Data Analyses), not treatment night alone.

Matches Effects on NPSG ¶2 (overall P = 0.001, omitted), Table 3 (shortened sleep REM 19.3 ± 3.4%) and the Figure 3 legend. Paper says 'beyond its sleep-disruptive effects'; the Discussion ¶1 states the shortened-sleep reasoning.

results.corrected_extracted: Recovery night with placebo after the MDMA session: total sleep 403.6 (SEM 34.4) minutes and REM 22.2% (1.5), against 431.9 minutes and 20.6% on the recovery night of the placebo session; no main effects of night and no night-by-drug interactions except for REM percentage, reduced on the treatment night only.
results.note: Values match Table 3. The paper also reports no night-by-drug interactions, so it did not show total sleep returning on the recovery night; those values are descriptive. Figure 3 legend adds a REM night effect (P = 0.001).

results.corrected_extracted: Only 7 completed; two withdrew and the 12-sequence Latin square was incomplete; the laboratory schedule was earlier than the participants' usual sleep times, which the authors judged unlikely to affect the MDMA-placebo comparison. The abstract states that MDMA reduced stage 3/4 sleep, which the drug comparison does not show (P = 0.119).
results.note: All else matches (Experimental Procedures ¶1; Discussion ¶9; Abstract). The authors tie the schedule to the user-control differences and call an effect on MDMA-placebo results unlikely; the anchor should carry that. Stage 3/4: 5.0 vs 5.7% (Table 3).

results.corrected_extracted: Treatment by day interaction F = 4.63 (df 2 and 12), P = 0.032; after shortened sleep the mean nap-test latency was shorter than after placebo (about 6 minutes, per the Discussion), while after MDMA it differed neither from placebo nor from shortened sleep, per the Results text; the Figure 4 legend instead reports shortened sleep as shorter than both placebo and MDMA (P = 0.031), and in the figure the MDMA bar is close to placebo; no differences on the day after the recovery night; sleep-onset REM periods 2.14 (shortened sleep), 1.43 (MDMA), 1.00 (placebo), not significant.
results.note: Numbers match the text, but the cited Figure 4 legend contradicts it (bars by eye: placebo about 15, MDMA 14, shortened sleep 7 minutes). Discussion ¶2 also claims shortened sleep raised sleepiness on both days, against the Results.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors conclude that MDMA's sleep loss was not associated with next-day sleepiness and that next-day sleep latency remained at placebo levels; with 7 participants, MDMA's next-day values were not significantly different from those after shortened sleep either, per the Results text (the Figure 4 legend reports the opposite).
results.corrected_locator: Abstract › Measurements and Results and Conclusions; Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results › Effects on the MSLT, 1st paragraph; Figure 4 legend
results.note: Conclusions confirmed in the Abstract and Discussion ¶1-2. The 'not different from shortened sleep' point comes from Results › Effects on the MSLT, not the cited places, and the Figure 4 legend contradicts it.

results.corrected_extracted: Effects generally significant by the 2-hour test (the first post-dose psychomotor test), maximal at 2 to 4 hours and decreasing at the 6-hour test, the last; DXM produced longer-lasting Balance and Circular Lights deficits than triazolam; at the penultimate and maximum DXM doses, deficits were still apparent at the last assessment; the highest doses sometimes produced complete impairment (scored 0).
results.note: 'Maximal over the following tests' misplaces the peak: the paper says 2 to 4 h, the first two psychomotor tests. Monitor ratings began at 30 min, so 'first post-dose test' fits psychomotor tests only. Test times are study conditions.

Matches Results › Emesis; the dose levels are 100, 200, 300 and 400+ mg/70 kg (study conditions). The paper's per-dose denominators at 600 and 700 conflict with Table 2 (8 and 4 people); not used here.

Abstract sentence, General Procedures ¶4 (questionnaires about 7 h after dosing 'when acute drug effects had resolved') and the 120/240/360-min psychomotor schedule all match; Discussion ¶7 is the safety paragraph. The erratum does not touch this.

General Procedures ¶5 and Data Analysis ¶1 match; the rule is failing both tasks 'at any single time point'. Results ¶1 gives the stop reasons: 7 impairment, 2 investigator judgement, 1 participant choice; 2 of 12 received every dose.

All figures match Persisting Effects Questionnaire ¶1-3 (another 3 of 12 put the experiences among the ten most meaningful). The questionnaire asked about experiences 'during any of the sessions', placebo sessions included.

results.corrected_extracted: One participant reached a stop point by declining that dose again and reported a post-session headache attributed to DXM; the primary monitor was reachable by phone throughout, no volunteer called or reported distress after the sessions, and no lasting distress or persisting perceptual phenomena were reported at the one-month follow-up.
results.note: Discussion ¶7 and Results ¶1: the stop point was the participant's choice not to receive that dose again; the paper reports the headache but does not give it as the reason. The rest matches.

Discussion ¶6 and Participants ¶2 match; the authors say preparation, support and setting 'seems likely' to have contributed. Exclusions also covered substance dependence, pregnancy or nursing, and contraindications to sedatives or anesthetics.

plain.fix: how 2: Trouble falling asleep was recorded nearly three times as often with the medicine as with the dummy pill. | how 3: Who recorded sleep problems, and whether a questionnaire was used, changed how big the difference looked. | how 4: A drug company paid for the review, and two of the authors work for its parent company.
plain.note: how 2 lacked the comparison group. how 3: elicited vs spontaneous reporting did not predict the RR; rater type and rating-scale use did; 'a lot' is unquantified. how 4: the paper never says the funder makes a compared medicine.

plain.fix: short: After MDMA, people slept about two hours less than with a dummy pill, and had very little dreaming (REM) sleep. | how 2: After MDMA they took much longer to fall asleep than after the dummy pill.
plain.note: The study measured REM sleep, not dreams; 437.1 vs 310.6 minutes is about 2.1 hours, an outcome, not a dose or timing. how 2 lacked the comparison group. Other lines match Table 3.

plain.fix: but: Only 7 people were tested, too few to rule out a difference. | how 2: After a short night in bed, they fell asleep faster than after a full night with the dummy pill. | how 3: After MDMA, they took about as long to fall asleep as after the dummy pill. | how 4: They were not asked how tired they felt, and mood and thinking were not tested the next day.
plain.note: Figure 4 puts MDMA (about 14 min) beside placebo (15), not in between; the Discussion says placebo levels. The short night also had a dummy pill. Nap tests measured sleepiness, not felt tiredness. 'See a real difference' presumes one.

plain.fix: short: After the highest doses, balance and coordination were still affected at the day's last test, while other effects were wearing off. | how 4: More than half vomited at least once at the higher doses.
plain.note: Effects were 'decreasing', not gone, at the last psychomotor test; 'acute effects had resolved' refers to later questionnaires. Deficits were reported at each person's two highest doses. Vomiting: 7 of 12 at least once; half or fewer at most doses.

plain.fix: but: Only 12 carefully chosen volunteers, in a calm lab; people with psychosis or bipolar illness, themselves or in close family, could not take part. | how 4: One person asked not to have that dose again; they had a headache after the session that they put down to DXM.
plain.note: Exclusion covered personal as well as immediate-family history. A stop point ends dose increases, not the study; it was the person's choice, and the paper does not give the headache as the reason. Short answer matches Discussion ¶7.

paper_notes.faraone_2019: Middle insomnia z printed as 183 (implausible). Figure 3 paragraph repeats Figure 2's Egger result (t = 0.37, p = 0.7) and cites 'Figure 4' for Figure 3. Absolute drug and placebo rates are not given in the text.
paper_notes.randall_2009: Internal conflicts: Figure 4 legend (shortened sleep shorter than placebo and MDMA, P = 0.031) vs Results text (MDMA not different from shortened sleep); Discussion ¶2 (shortened sleep raised sleepiness on both days) vs Results (no day-3 difference); Figure 2 legend P values (MDMA vs placebo P = 0.001, shortened sleep P = 0.031) vs text (MDMA vs placebo P = 0.031, shortened sleep P = 0.005); Abstract's stage 3/4 claim unsupported. No funding anchor: NIH grant R01-DA14874; 'not an industry-supported study'; Johanson employed by CRS Associates LLC.
paper_notes.reissig_2012: Emesis denominators at 600 and 700 conflict with Table 2. No funding anchor: NIDA grant DA003889; Carter an employee of Jazz Pharmaceuticals with stock options.
